1.point: Prostration, the posture of annihilation we take twice a rak'a, opens onto the fourth stage, passing away; the chapter will say what is lost, what is found and how the traveller returns.
steps: Hook: prostration is the one act done twice and a scholar calls it the posture of annihilation in God.
That annihilation is fana', the state the traveller reaches only at the end of the road.
Recall in a sentence where the road stood: stage three adorned the heart and love brought the traveller to the door.
State what the chapter establishes: what is lost, what is found, how the traveller comes back.

2.point: Before God's glory the traveller stops perceiving himself; since his soul remains and he does not become God, what he loses is only a false, self-standing self.
steps: Glory arrives at the height of adorning and takes all the traveller's attention, including his sense of himself.
So passing away is a change in perception, not in what exists; the world goes on.
The traveller's soul also remains; this is not the Buddhist ending of the individual, since only an individual can taste anything.
Nor does the traveller become God; merging is impossible and claiming it is kufr.
Therefore what goes is the illusory self that stands apart from God, the last thing emptying left behind.

3.point: Passing away unfolds in three degrees, in action, attributes and essence, and each turns a formula the believer already recites into something he sees.
steps: Three veils (action, attributes, essence) give three degrees, unveiled from the outside in.
Degree one, in action: the power in every act is God's; this is la hawla wa la quwwata illa billah, lived rather than merely reasoned.
Degree two, in attributes: life, knowledge and power everywhere are His; this is la ilaha illa Allah, since Allah gathers all the attributes.
Degree three, in essence: only His glory remains and the one word left is Huwa, He.

4.point: Passing away is the beginning, not the end: the healthy outcome, reached by walking at the right pace, is a sober return in which the traveller is himself again and sees God and creation without either veiling the other.
steps: The station is the summit, not the end, and nearness is not safety.
Some do not come back well: lost for ever, lost for a while and uttering shath, or unable to tell self from God from creation and falling into licence.
All three have one cause, haste; balanced practice under law, guide and measured pace raises the traveller gradually.
The healthy return is sobriety after obliteration, grace bringing the traveller back to himself, telling himself from God and God from creation again.
This sobriety is higher than passing away, not a step down; the Imams lived in it and kept every law.
In it neither God nor creation veils the other; the traveller keeps both unity and plurality.

¶1.label: advance
¶1.why: The hook: prostration as the posture of annihilation, with Tabrizi's words. Nothing before it; the section cannot open without it.

¶2.label: advance
¶2.why: Turns the hook into the chapter's subject (fana'), recalls stage three in two sentences and states the three things the chapter will establish. Does exactly what the opening point asks.

¶3.label: advance
¶3.why: Supplies the first step: glory arrives and takes the traveller's attention, including his sense of himself. The fear/joy comparison is used within the paragraph to make the mechanism credible.

¶4.label: advance
¶4.why: Draws the consequence that passing away is epistemological, a change in perception not in existence; the world goes on. Needed before the soul and the non-merging claims can be made.

¶5.label: advance
¶5.why: New step: the soul remains, against the nirvana reading. The argument that only an individual can taste anything is used, not merely cited.

¶6.label: advance
¶6.why: New step on the other side: the traveller does not become God. Together with ¶5 it closes both wrong readings so ¶7 can name what is actually lost.

¶7.label: advance
¶7.why: Delivers the section's conclusion: what is lost is the false, self-standing self, the last residue of emptying, and the real self is returned. The point lands here.

¶8.label: restate
¶8.why: Repeats ¶7 (false self lost), ¶4-5 (soul and world remain) and ¶6 (no merging) in three sentences. The conclusion was already stated once in ¶7.

¶9.label: advance
¶9.why: Supplies the frame: three veils give three degrees in a set order, and announces that each turns words we say into something seen. Every later paragraph hangs on this.

¶10.label: advance
¶10.why: First degree, in action, tied to la hawla wa la quwwata illa billah. Also plants the power/intention distinction that ¶24 later uses.

¶11.label: support
¶11.why: The recipe/dish contrast is what gives 'lived truth' its meaning: any believer can reason out that there is no power but God's; the traveller tastes it. The point's claim that each degree is words 'lived' leans on this. Borderline: ¶12 and ¶14 would still read without it.

¶12.label: advance
¶12.why: Second degree, in attributes, tied to la ilaha illa Allah with the reason (Allah gathers all attributes). A step the point needs.

¶13.label: support
¶13.why: Glosses the Throne Verse so that the verse actually serves the attribute of life, then extends it to the other attributes. Its last sentence repeats ¶12, so the paragraph is thin, but the verse would hang unexplained without the first two.

¶14.label: advance
¶14.why: Third degree, in essence, tied to the word Huwa and Surah al-Ikhlas. The last step of the three.

¶15.label: aside
¶15.why: The Badr hadith is a second illustration of Huwa on believing lips after Surah al-Ikhlas has already done that job. No later sentence uses Khidr, the dream or the battle; cutting it loses nothing the argument needs.

¶16.label: aside
¶16.why: A second scholar counting four degrees instead of three. The section neither adopts the fourth degree nor resolves the difference; it is a footnote-grade remark that the point does not need.

¶17.label: aside
¶17.why: Returns to the Munajat Sha'baniyyah to tie the last degree to the book's opening line. A pleasing echo, but the three-degree point is already complete at ¶14; nothing after it depends on this paragraph except ¶18, which it exists to set up.

¶18.label: restate
¶18.why: Its claim, that the soul held by God's glory has not dissolved and is still there, was made in Section 2 (¶5). It re-argues the soul-remains point through the quotation rather than adding a step to the three degrees.

¶19.label: restate
¶19.why: A summary of ¶9-14: three degrees and the three formulas. The conclusion was stated in ¶9 and delivered degree by degree.

¶20.label: advance
¶20.why: First step: the station is a summit not an end, and nearness is not safety. Satan's fall is used to establish that danger persists at the summit, which ¶21-25 build on.

¶21.label: advance
¶21.why: Supplies the step that the return can fail and that three failures follow, treated as principles. Thin, two sentences of framing, but ¶22-24 are unintelligible as 'first, second, third' without it.

¶22.label: advance
¶22.why: First failure: the traveller stays lost. The accident comparison is used to explain why outcomes differ. A new item the point needs.

¶23.label: advance
¶23.why: Second failure: temporary loss, shath, and the rejected claim that duties lapse for ever. New item; the duty question feeds ¶27's note that the Imams kept every law.

¶24.label: advance
¶24.why: Third and worst failure: licence, with the power/intention distinction from ¶10 brought back to explain the error. Tabatabai's list is a second voice, but the paragraph's own step is new.

¶25.label: advance
¶25.why: Diagnoses the one cause (haste) and names the remedy (balanced practice under law, guide and pace), which is what makes the healthy return possible. The forward references to other chapters are the only loose weight.

¶26.label: advance
¶26.why: Defines the healthy return: sobriety after obliteration, grace bringing the traveller back to himself, telling himself from God again. The core of the point.

¶27.label: advance
¶27.why: Establishes that this return is higher than the state it returns from, with the Imams as the standard. Without it the 'healthy outcome' could read as a consolation prize; the point needs it.

¶28.label: advance
¶28.why: Supplies the last clause of the point: in sobriety neither God nor creation veils the other. Amuli's gnostic is a second witness, but the paragraph's own step (both kept, neither veiled) is new.

¶29.label: restate
¶29.why: Its first two sentences summarise ¶20-28 (beginning not end, loss of false self, sober return). Only the third sentence, setting up Imam Ali's saying, adds anything, and it introduces a quotation rather than a step.

¶30.label: restate
¶30.why: Glosses the quotation to say the world and the looker both remain and nothing hides God, which is ¶28's claim in other words.

¶31.label: aside
¶31.why: A transition raising a question the chapter does not answer (where the road came from, who walked it first). It adds no link to the section's point; it belongs to the next chapter's opening.
